clue.text: In retrospect, ChatGPT etc destructive, vacuous at heart? There's a notion

indicators.note: Looking at something in retrospect is running your eye back over what has already gone past, so the pair of letters arrives in the opposite order.
A vacuous remark has nothing in the middle of it, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends and loses everything between them.

parts.note: ChatGPT and its rivals are all artificial intelligence, and 'etc' asks for the class rather than the one product

indicators.note: What sits at the heart of a thing is buried in the very centre of it, so this piece goes between the other two rather than beside them.

parts.note: hollowed out, the word keeps only its outer letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'In retrospect' looks like an essayist clearing his throat before an opinion. It is an instruction, and so is every other word before the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: a notion: the everyday synonym, in the sense of a thought that has occurred to someone rather than a settled plan or a whim.

clue.text: Food guru initiated reforms

indicators.note: A reform takes an institution apart and puts it back together in a different shape, which is exactly what happens to these nine letters.

parts.note: nine letters in and nine out, with three Is among them to place

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a wellness company announcing changes, and 'initiated reforms' reads as one achievement — which is what hides the fact that the first of those words is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Food guru: a dietitian is the trained authority people take their eating advice from, so 'guru' names that role loosely rather than any religious one.

clue.text: Short time enthralled by wild iguana somewhere in W Indies

indicators.note: enthralled means held captive, so the time letter is held inside the rearranged lizard
wild means the letters of iguana run loose into a new order

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone is briefly captivated by a free-roaming lizard on a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges IGUANA to ANIGUA, and 'enthralled by' sets the T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Antigua is an island in the Leeward Islands of the Caribbean, part of Antigua and Barbuda.

clue.text: Strings of buckwheat, Asian primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening character of each word in the run is kept.

parts.note: four words, four initials, taken in the order they are written

explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: the sentence is a description of the thing and the recipe for spelling it at the same time, which is why nothing is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: these are thin Japanese noodles made from buckwheat flour, so every word of the description is true of the dish named.

clue.text: Man alternately bites dog

parts.note: to man a desk is to staff it — the verb, not the noun

indicators.note: Doing something alternately means every other one, so the reader keeps a letter, skips the next and carries on to the end.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters, where the counting lands

explanation.walkthrough: 'Man bites dog' is the old newsroom test of what counts as news, and the clue leaves that picture intact. A staffie is Britain's pet name for a Staffordshire bull terrier.
explanation.definitionFit: dog: the answer is one breed, so the plain category word defines it by example, which the exact wordplay makes fair.

clue.text: What musician may take regularly: mike for musician

parts.note: a performer takes one at the end of a set, and a string player takes one in hand

indicators.note: Letters taken at a regular interval means at a steady step through the word, and the step here is every second one.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of the microphone's short name

explanation.walkthrough: The setter uses 'musician' twice on purpose: the first one is wordplay and the last one defines. The trap is treating the whole opening phrase as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: musician: a definition by example, since the answer is the surname of one particular singer rather than a word meaning any player of music.

clue.text: Exchange whip

definitions.meaning: the verb sense: two things trade places, or you move from one to the other
a thin flexible rod cut from a tree and used for beating — the noun sense

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, no indicator, nothing to shuffle. A verb and a noun set side by side, with the clue refusing to say which of them is doing the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: Exchange is the verb, to trade one thing for another; whip is the noun, a springy cane for striking, and one six-letter word carries both.

clue.text: Rained heavily — wearing fur?

definitions.meaning: rain coming down hard is said to do this, hammering on the roof
a pelt is an animal's skin with the fur still on it, so a creature in one is described by the same six letters

explanation.walkthrough: The dash joins two senses with nothing in common. The first is the ordinary weather word; the question mark on the second admits that it is the setter playing.
explanation.definitionFit: Rained heavily is the weather sense, hammering down; wearing fur? works off the noun, since a pelt is a hide, so an animal in one qualifies.

clue.text: In the raw with the bananas — extremely chaste

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the five words before it go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone naked with the fruit claims to be utterly pure, a comic picture of innocence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit beside a naked person, but it is the signal to rearrange INTHERAWWITHTHE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone morally spotless, beyond reproach, which matches being extremely chaste or pure.

clue.text: Grim perm an entertainer hides in passing

indicators.note: Something hiding in a place is already sitting there in plain view, so the letters are written out inside those words and need only picking up.

parts.note: eleven consecutive letters running across four words, beginning part-way into the first

explanation.walkthrough: A grim perm and an entertainer make an odd little picture, which is the giveaway: Everyman is not describing anything here, only supplying letters for the run to cross.
explanation.definitionFit: passing: the fleeting sense rather than the moving-by one — a passing fashion is one that will not last, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: I'm in favour of six heads of state issuing numbing generalisations departing from script

parts.note: the clue's own contraction, taken at face value
to be pro something is to be in favour of it
the Roman numeral for six

indicators.note: The head of a word is its front, so each of the four words that follow gives up nothing but its opening letter.

parts.note: four initials in the order the words appear

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a politician saying nothing at length. 'Heads of state' reads as one phrase — presidents and prime ministers — and prising it apart is the whole trick.
explanation.definitionFit: departing from script: an actor who leaves the written lines is making them up on the spot, which is what the answer names.

clue.text: Knocking off chocolate sauce perhaps

definitions.meaning: British slang for killing someone, the same underworld register as the clue's own phrase
whatever is poured over the top of a pudding, of which the sauce is one instance

explanation.walkthrough: Two idioms with nothing in common but their letters, and the clue slides from one to the other without a join. 'Perhaps' is the flag that the sauce is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Knocking off is the slang verb for killing; chocolate sauce perhaps is a definition by example of anything spooned over a dessert.

clue.text: Give gratuity to a little fellow over in seedy venue

indicators.note: Something turned over lands the other way up, so the three pieces are read back to front once they have been laid end to end.

parts.note: the few coins left for a waiter
the clue's own letter, joining the pieces either side of it
the small chap of folklore, three letters of him

explanation.walkthrough: A fleapit is British for a shabby old cinema, the sort whose seats you would rather not inspect too closely. The surface, a tip for a small waiter, is pure decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: seedy venue: the word names a grubby, run-down cinema or theatre, so the definition describes its condition rather than any particular building.

clue.text: Raunchier, but laughably so? That's a big blow

indicators.note: laughably so says the word before is made ridiculous, its letters thrown into a comic jumble

explanation.surface: Something is raunchier, but only in a ridiculous way, followed by a remark about a big blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laughably so' looks like a comment on how raunchy something is, but it rearranges RAUNCHIER. 'Big blow' sounds like a punch; here it is a storm wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical cyclone with extremely strong winds is literally a very big blow of air.

clue.text: Empty after having had nothing — like an egg?

indicators.note: Coming after something means standing behind it, so the piece named first in the clue is written second in the grid.

parts.note: O is the zero on any scoreboard, so nothing is a circle
an empty space is a void — a plain synonym, not an instruction

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is 'Empty' at the front, which reads as an order to hollow a word out. It is a synonym, and the clue is a plain two-part build.
explanation.definitionFit: like an egg?: egg-shaped, the adjective for a solid narrower at one end, with the question mark admitting the definition works by resemblance.

clue.text: Proposers involved tormentor

indicators.note: An involved story is a tangled one, and letters tangled together are no longer in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: nine letters with two Ps, two Rs, two Ss and two Os to find places for

explanation.walkthrough: Two abstract nouns with one soft word between them: 'involved' has to be the signal, because neither noun can possibly define the other.
explanation.definitionFit: tormentor: one who inflicts suffering on people under their power, the systematic and continuing kind rather than a single act of cruelty.

clue.text: Unattractive lowland

definitions.meaning: the kind adjective for a face nobody would call handsome
a broad flat stretch of open country — the noun sense

explanation.walkthrough: Two words and no machinery at all. They share a spelling and nothing else: one describes a face, the other a landscape, and neither is flagged as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Unattractive is the adjective used of a face; lowland is the noun, a wide flat tract of land, and one five-letter word covers both.

clue.text: Cool Prime Minister circumventing hot Member

indicators.note: To circumvent something is to go all the way round it, so the pair of letters opens up and the rest of the wordplay sits between them.

parts.note: PM is the standard shortening for the head of a British government
H is the tap marked hot, and the letter does that duty throughout crosswords
a member is a limb — an arm or a leg, and here the three-letter one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' beside a Prime Minister reads as an MP, and it is a limb. The definition is the old medicine: this is the humour that gave English the word phlegmatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Cool: the noun, as in keeping your cool — composure under pressure, which is the calm temperament the word names away from the medical sense.

clue.text: Merrily I open butts of French Pomerol to imbibe?

definitions.text: Merrily I open butts of French Pomerol to imbibe?

indicators.note: Merry is the polite old word for tipsy, and letters handled in that state do not stay where they were put.

parts.note: five letters lifted straight out of the clue, waiting to be shaken

indicators.note: A butt is the tail end of a thing, so each of the words that follow surrenders nothing but its final letter.

parts.note: the last letter of each of those four words, in the order they are written

explanation.walkthrough: Pomerol is a red from Bordeaux, so the surface is a wine buff's confession — and every word of that confession is also machinery, which is what makes it an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: someone who cheerfully opens good French wine to drink it is precisely what this Greek-rooted word for a wine lover names.

clue.text: Riding, it seems, with son going up to the coast

indicators.note: with says the son is put back among the remaining letters, higher up than before
in a down entry, going up lifts the son out of his place lower in the column

parts.note: someone riding appears to be on horse

explanation.surface: A rider and their son are heading uphill on the way to the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: Riding is ON HORSE; 'going up' lifts its S (son) out, leaving ONHORE, and 'with' sets S back in higher up the column, after ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Onshore describes movement from the sea towards land, as an onshore wind blows to the coast.

clue.text: Journalistic chap seen in every direction: gee!

parts.note: north, east, west and south — the four compass points, in the order that spells them
both are exclamations of mild surprise: 'Gee!' and 'Man!' do the same job in speech

explanation.walkthrough: The compass in that order is one of the oldest devices in the craft and worth owning outright. The second half is a swap of one exclamation for another.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalistic chap: the definition splits neatly in two, 'journalistic' supplying the trade and 'chap' insisting on a man rather than a reporter of either sex.

clue.text: In the E End, loathes rowers

indicators.note: the East End of London is famous for its Cockney accent, which drops the H, so the word is pronounced in that voice

parts.note: to loathe something is to hate it

explanation.surface: Someone from the East End hates something, a scrap of London local colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the E End' means in a Cockney voice, which drops the H of HATES, giving 'ATES, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eights are eight-oared racing boats and their crews, so the word names groups of rowers.

clue.text: Third character in John Cleese play, Drains

indicators.note: In the surface 'play' is a noun, a piece of theatre; as the instruction it is the verb for messing about with a thing, and letters played with land in a new order.

parts.note: J, O, H — count three characters into the name and stop
the comedian's surname, six letters to be rearranged with the one above

explanation.walkthrough: 'Third character' invites you to count actors rather than letters, and the definition is the last word rather than the play's title it is dressed up as.
explanation.definitionFit: Drains: to leech is to drain something steadily away — blood from a patient, money from a friend — so the verbs agree in the third person.

clue.text: Time for you and me, did you say?

definitions.note: The answer is a plural count noun and 'Time' is a mass noun: the setter is defining the units by the thing they measure, which both English and the crossword allow.

indicators.note: Asking whether that is what you said points at the sound of the words rather than their spelling, which is the whole instruction here.

parts.note: what belongs to you and me is ours, and an unsounded aitch at the front is all that separates that from the spelling wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Everything is in the question mark: read as a statement the clue makes no sense, and read as a question it is asking you to listen. The H is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Time: the answer is the unit time is counted in, so the definition names the whole of which the answer supplies the measured parts.

clue.text: Small, small sound: sound of sorrow

parts.note: the Scottish word for small, and a fixture of these puzzles
the little noise a microwave makes when it finishes

explanation.walkthrough: The repetition is the disguise: 'small' is used twice for two different jobs and 'sound' twice for two more. Only the last three words define.
explanation.definitionFit: sound of sorrow: crying aloud in grief, so the definition names the noise itself rather than the feeling that produces it.

clue.text: Avoid Everyman's daft appearance: begone!

parts.note: to get out of a duty is to avoid it
the setter signs every puzzle Everyman, so his own possessive is the two letters MY
someone who looks a sight looks ridiculous

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman puts himself in nearly every puzzle he sets, and the possessive is always MY. Once you have that, the outer pieces are two ordinary phrases laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: begone!: an order to leave at once, which is what the fifteen-letter phrase says in blunter and more modern English.

clue.text: Geographical feature that is around small lake? The reverse!

definitions.text: Geographical feature that is around small lake? The reverse!

indicators.note: around means the letters for 'that is' go round the others

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for 'that is'
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A geography question about something circling a little lake, quickly corrected: it is the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay puts IE round SL; 'The reverse!' then turns the picture over for the definition, since the lake is really round the island, not the island round the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: An isle is a small island, a piece of land with water all round it.

clue.text: Tyrant, somewhat ungenerous

indicators.note: Somewhat means partly, so only a part of the word beside it is wanted — the letters that sit consecutively inside it.

parts.note: four consecutive letters inside the long word at the end, and finding where they start is the job

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman finishes with a gift: an emperor whose name has been a byword for cruelty since the first century, sitting untouched inside a word about meanness.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyrant: the emperor who is said to have fiddled while Rome burned stands for despotic rule, so the general word defines the name by example.
